solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Citizen, bound to be heard, large landowner (8,5)

indicatorNotes.to be heard: what is heard is a sound, so we want a word that sounds like 'bound'

blocks.note: a national is a citizen of a country

annotation.surface: A description of a landed citizen who is duty-bound to be listened to.
annotation.walkthrough: The National Trust is a British conservation charity that owns vast stretches of countryside and many stately homes, making it one of the country's largest landowners.
annotation.definitionFit: The National Trust owns more land than almost anyone else in Britain.

entries.clue: Lacking staff an advantage at times (3,3,5)

blocks.note: a wand is a rod or staff

annotation.surface: An understaffed business finding that its short-handedness sometimes helps.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but here it is a stick: NO WAND is being without a staff.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrase: something that happens occasionally, not all the time, happens at times.

entries.clue: Point about author raised over time (5)

indicatorNotes.about: the point goes around the author
indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, raising a word turns it upside down, so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: PT is the abbreviation for point
the author of a clue refers to themself as ME
O = over, the cricket scoring abbreviation

annotation.surface: Someone making a point about a writer, raised over time.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole of point-about-author is turned over, not just the author. O for over is cricket scoring shorthand, and in music time means the speed of a piece.
annotation.definitionFit: Tempo is the time or pace at which music is played.

entries.clue: Big Oil and BAT playing essential parts (9)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters are played with, rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder; BAT is British American Tobacco

annotation.surface: The oil majors and a big tobacco firm playing essential roles in the economy.
annotation.walkthrough: An obbligato is a musical accompaniment that must not be left out; the Italian plural is obbligati. 'Playing' looks like corporate play but is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Obbligati are instrumental parts a composer marks as indispensable, so essential parts.

entries.clue: God elevated Dail member and writer in style (3,4)

indicatorNotes.elevated: in a down clue, lifting a word up reverses it

blocks.note: a TD (Teachta Dála) is a member of the Dáil, the Irish parliament

annotation.surface: A god, an Irish politician and a novelist sharing a sense of style.
annotation.walkthrough: The Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament and its members are TDs.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a named design movement of the 1920s and 1930s is one particular style among many.

entries.clue: Bone set in hospital usually (5)

indicatorNotes.set in: the answer is set inside the following words

annotation.surface: A broken bone is normally set in hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'set' a medical verb, but it is telling you the bone is set into the next two words. The talus is the ankle bone.
annotation.definitionFit: The talus is the bone at the top of the foot that forms the ankle joint.

entries.clue: Bore in one Parisian river (9)

blocks.note: the Derwent, a river in England

annotation.surface: Somebody tedious on the banks of a Paris river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a dull person but is the past tense of bear, as in bore the pain. The Derwent is one of several English rivers of that name.
annotation.definitionFit: To have borne something is to have undergone it: bore = underwent.

entries.clue: Prominent feature from Left? (3)

blocks.note: reads as a striking characteristic; it is a feature of the landscape that stands up high
reads as a political origin; it is the start of the stock phrase 'from left to right', which wants its missing half

annotation.surface: A striking characteristic that originated on the political left.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'from Left' is half a phrase: its partner, TO R(ight), is the answer. A tor is a rocky hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: A rocky peak rising above moorland is a prominent landscape feature, and it is also what follows 'from L'.

entries.clue: Periodically saw firms float (4)

indicatorNotes.Periodically: take letters at regular periods, every other one

annotation.surface: Occasionally one sees companies go public.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about business: to float a firm is to sell its shares on the stock market.
annotation.definitionFit: To float in water is to swim, or at least to stay up in it.

entries.clue: Struggled rather to concede first lost game (10)

indicatorNotes.to concede first: the word gives up its first letter

blocks.note: rather = MORE, which loses its first letter M

annotation.surface: A player struggled and preferred to concede the opening game, which was lost.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lost game' reads as a defeat, but it is a game nobody plays any more: battledore and shuttlecock was the forerunner of badminton. 'Rather' means more, as in more willing.
annotation.definitionFit: Battledore is an old racket game, a lost game in the sense of forgotten.

entries.clue: Pub-o’clock, getting round in very quickly (2,2,4)

indicatorNotes.getting: 'getting in' a round is taking it inside, as when you get a round of drinks in
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the round inside the pub-and-time pair, between the two

annotation.surface: When it's time for the pub, someone gets a round in fast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pub o'clock' is jokey slang for the hour to start drinking, and 'round' pretends to be a round of drinks; it is only the letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: In no time means almost instantly, very quickly.

entries.clue: Street artist needing iron to make raking fire (6)

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

annotation.surface: A graffiti artist who needs a hot iron to get a fire going.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a street artist stoking a fire; the words are simply three abbreviations in a row.
annotation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with sweeping machine-gun fire, typically from low-flying aircraft.

entries.clue: Cut the French introduced to suit Goethe’s heroine (5,6)

indicatorNotes.introduced to: one word is put inside another

blocks.note: Mignon is the girl in Goethe's novel Wilhelm Meister

annotation.surface: A French tailor's cut introduced to dress a Goethe heroine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' and 'suit' both suggest tailoring, but the cut is of beef.
annotation.definitionFit: Filet mignon is a prized cut of beef from the tenderloin.

entries.clue: Bear devouring unruly lad as punishment (4,6)

indicatorNotes.devouring: one word eats another, holding it inside

blocks.note: to harbour, as in harbour a grudge, is to bear it

annotation.surface: A bear eating an unruly boy as punishment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is not the animal but the verb: to harbour, bear or hold.
annotation.definitionFit: Hard labour was a prison sentence of heavy physical work.

entries.clue: Ruin beginning to show in desperate couple (9)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: only the beginning of 'show' is wanted, its first letter
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the S inside the desperate word, breaking it open

annotation.surface: A couple in trouble whose ruin is starting to be visible.
annotation.walkthrough: The desperate word is split open for the letter, so the break falls inside it rather than between the two words of the couple.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a building that has decayed through neglect is in ruin.

entries.clue: Kingdom where fruitarians peeled bananas? (9)

indicatorNotes.bananas: slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: FRUITARIANS loses its outer F and S

annotation.surface: A land where fruit-only eaters peel their bananas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peeled bananas' makes a perfect fruitarian breakfast; in fact 'peeled' works on fruitarians and 'bananas' means crazy. Ruritania is the invented kingdom in Anthony Hope's The Prisoner of Zenda.
annotation.definitionFit: Ruritania is a fictional Central European kingdom.

entries.clue: Woman has everyone back on MDMA (4)

indicatorNotes.back: reading everyone back means writing it from its end to its start
indicatorNotes.on: in an across clue, one thing 'on' another comes after it, so the reversed word follows the drug

blocks.note: MDMA is ecstasy, known as E

annotation.surface: A woman gets everybody back on ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' puts the reversed ALL after E.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the answer is a woman's first name, as borne by the singer Fitzgerald.

entries.clue: Spoils of War? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'of War?' points to the god of war, so Mars is war personified

blocks.note: a verb here: damages or ruins
the Roman god whose domain was war

annotation.surface: The plunder taken in a war.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spoils of war' is a stock phrase for booty, but 'Spoils' is a verb and 'of War' is the god's title.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain: to mar is to spoil, and the Roman god of war stands for war itself.

entries.clue: Not willing to accept Republican way for America (10)

indicatorNotes.to accept: the word takes the letter inside it

annotation.surface: Someone refusing to accept a Republican path for the United States.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not willing' reads as reluctant, but it means without a will: someone who dies intestate leaves none.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the US federal highway network links the states, so it is a road, a way, for America.

entries.clue: Flyer soon welcomed by workers’ association (7)

indicatorNotes.welcomed by: taken in by, so it goes inside

annotation.surface: A leaflet shortly to be welcomed by a union.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flyer' looks like a leaflet but is a bird: the tinamou is a ground bird of Central and South America.
annotation.definitionFit: A tinamou is a bird, and birds are flyers.

entries.clue: Releasing uranium, home visitor’s put away (6)

indicatorNotes.Releasing: letting go of the letter, so it is removed

blocks.note: U is the chemical symbol for uranium, removed from GUEST

annotation.surface: A radioactive house guest being locked up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put away' is slang for eating a lot, as in he put away three pies.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to put food away is colloquial for eating it, taking it into the body.

entries.clue: Retire having abandoned one North European city (5)

indicatorNotes.having abandoned: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so the N is left out of the phrase

blocks.note: to turn in is to go to bed, to retire
N = North; one of the two Ns is dropped

annotation.surface: Someone retiring and leaving a northern European city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'North European' looks like one phrase, but 'one North' goes with the deletion and the city is simply European.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the answer is one city in Europe, the Piedmont capital in northern Italy.

entries.clue: NZ Rail in evil nonsense about going westward (8)

indicatorNotes.going westward: in an across clue, going west means reading right to left

annotation.surface: Bad nonsense about a railway line in New Zealand heading west.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rail' looks like a railway, but it is the bird family: the notornis, or takahe, is a flightless rail from New Zealand.
annotation.definitionFit: Notornis is the genus of the takahe, a New Zealand rail.

entries.clue: Sage from Dublin bringing down leader? (5)

indicatorNotes.bringing down leader: in a down clue, the first letter moves to the bottom

blocks.note: someone from Dublin is Irish; I moves from the top to the bottom

annotation.surface: A wise person from Dublin who topples a leader.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bringing down leader' suggests a coup, and the question mark nods to Rishi Sunak, a British prime minister; here it only moves the I to the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A borrowing from Sanskrit: in Hindu tradition an inspired poet-seer goes by this title, so it names a sage.

entries.clue: Trooper left ragtag army in Irish county (10)

indicatorNotes.ragtag: disorderly, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.in: the letters go inside the county

blocks.note: Cavan, a county in the Republic of Ireland

annotation.surface: A soldier deserted a ramshackle army in Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as deserted, but it is just L.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a trooper is a private soldier in a mounted regiment, a horse soldier.

entries.clue: Commercials Saudis used at regular intervals (3)

indicatorNotes.at regular intervals: letters taken at a fixed, repeating spacing, here every second one

annotation.surface: Saudi Arabia running television adverts regularly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Used' only joins: the Saudis' letters are used at regular intervals.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, shortened: adverts on TV or radio are commercials.

entries.clue: Degenerate son with tattoos (4)

annotation.surface: A dissolute son covered in tattoos.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Degenerate' looks like an adjective or noun describing the son, but it is the verb: to degenerate is to sink.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to degenerate is to decline morally, to go downhill.

entries.clue: Restrictive practice a signal to turn nasty (13)

indicatorNotes.nasty: the letters take a bad turn

annotation.surface: A restrictive work rule that is a warning sign things are about to get ugly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Restrictive practice' is a trade-union term for rules limiting output; here it is taken literally, as squeezing a throat.
annotation.definitionFit: Strangulation restricts the airway, a restrictive practice in the literal sense.
